Started as notes for my intro talk before "The Big Combo", grew into a general crib sheet. I'm not a DP. I've lit two music videos and one short, badly, then less badly.

## Three-point lighting, the boring base

Key, fill, back. Key at 45 degrees to the subject and above eye line, fill on the other side at a lower level, back light behind to separate them from the background. Every textbook. Useful mainly so you know what you're breaking.

## Key-to-fill ratio

The mood dial. 2:1 is a sitcom. 4:1 is drama. 8:1 and above is noir. On the Kirsty Duncan video for "Saltcoats" (shot December 2024) we ran about 6:1, key through a 90 cm octabox, fill from a white bounce card, nothing else.

## John Alton

"Painting with Light" (1949), the DP's own book. Shot "The Big Combo" (1955) and "T-Men" (1947). His rule: light the shadows, not the faces. One hard source per shot, from below or the side, and let the rest go black. Smoke or fog to make the beam visible. See the screening notes in [[Film noir watchlist]].

## Practicals and motivated light

A practical is a lamp you can see in the shot. Motivated light means the light pretends to come from somewhere real: a window, a street lamp, a fridge. In our short ("The Last Tram to Auchenshuggle", see [[Screenwriting structure]]) the only motivation inside the tram at night would be the ceiling strips, so we'll fake them with two Aputure MC panels at 3200K tucked above the windows.

## Colour temperature

- Tungsten 3200K, warm.
- Daylight 5600K, cooler.
- Mixing both on purpose: warm interior, blue window. Classic night look.
- Gels: CTO (orange) to warm a daylight source, CTB (blue) to cool tungsten. 1/2 CTB on the window light for "Saltcoats".

## Golden hour and blue hour

Golden hour after sunrise and before sunset, low warm side light. Blue hour just after sunset, maybe 20 minutes in Glasgow in winter, longer in June. Terrence Malick shot most of "Days of Heaven" (1978) in that window. Néstor Almendros won the Oscar for it.

## Mistakes

- Pointed the key straight at someone wearing glasses. Reflection in both lenses. Raised the light, tilted the glasses down 5 degrees.
- Forgot a back light on a dark-haired actor against a dark wall. Head disappeared. Added a rim light at 1/4 power.
- Mixed LED panels from two brands, skin went green on one side. Stick to one brand or correct with 1/8 plus green.
